1. Model consistently overestimates prices in the early part of the 30-day horizon, especially after recent spikes — reduce initial forecast values by 1–3% to align with observed mean reversion.

2. Model tends to overshoot after sharp upward moves (e.g., 60→68), then undercorrects — apply a “cool-down” penalty: reduce forecast by 2–5% for the next 3–5 days post-spike.

3. Forecast mean is typically 2–4% higher than true outcome — apply a global downward bias correction of 2–3% for all 30-day forecasts.

4. Model underestimates late-period prices (last 7–10 days) — increase forecast by 1–3% for days 20–30 to capture momentum or policy-driven surges.

5. Forecast lags true outcome by 1–3 days — adjust for lag by shifting forecast values forward by 1–2 days (or apply a 1-day smoothing filter) to reduce delay.

6. Avoid overfitting to recent history — if last 5–7 days are volatile, reduce forecast sensitivity to those values; use 10–15 day rolling average for stabilization.
